Rep. Dina Titus Urges House GOP to Fast-Track a Fix to the Gambling Loss Tax Deduction

Published November 7, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Nevada Rep. Dina Titus sent a letter this past week to House Speaker Mike Johnson and Majority Leader Steve Scalise, urging them to attach a fix for the gambling-loss tax deduction to must-pass, end-of-year legislation before Congress runs out of time on the 2026 tax year.

What changed, and why it matters to bettors

Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed into law in 2025, the deduction gamblers can claim against their winnings for documented losses was cut from 100% to 90%, effective with the 2026 tax year. The practical effect shows up even for a bettor who breaks exactly even: someone who wins $100,000 over the year and loses $100,000 back would, under the 90% cap, still owe tax on $10,000 of income that was never actually profit. Titus argues the change "unfairly burdens professional gamblers and casual players alike."

The vehicle for a fix is already moving — slowly

A restoration of the full 100% deduction is written into Section 701 of the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act (HR 10357), which the House Ways and Means Committee already passed by a 38-5 vote on September 16. Titus points to that lopsided, bipartisan margin as evidence the fix has support across party lines — the holdup is getting it to the House floor, or folded into another bill leadership is willing to move, before the year ends. Titus has pushed this issue since shortly after the original cap became law, introducing her own bill, the FAIR BET Act, in 2025. A Senate companion, the FULL HOUSE Act from Sens. Ted Cruz, Catherine Cortez Masto, Bill Hagerty, and Jacky Rosen, has been introduced but hasn't moved.

Industry backing and the timeline problem

Titus says the push has backing from the American Gaming Association and operators including MGM, FanDuel, DraftKings, Caesars, and Wynn, who argue the cap pushes bettors toward offshore and unregulated platforms and reduces the tax revenue and jobs tied to the regulated industry. The timing is tight: the House returns from recess on November 9, and any fix still has to clear both the House and Senate before reaching the president's desk. The committee-passed language would apply retroactively to January 1, 2026, but if Congress doesn't act before year's end, gamblers filing 2026 returns would do so under the reduced 90% deduction regardless of what happens afterward.
